Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
At 44, Rafiq Khan had been in the United States long enough to build a life that looked steady from the outside. He lived alone, worked long hours as a chef, and was known in his restaurant kitchen as careful, polite, and unusually accommodating. What brought him to treatment now was not a new crisis so much as the exhaustion of living in a state of readiness that never fully lifted. He said he was tired of always scanning, tired of arranging himself around danger, and most of all tired of feeling like the man who survived had become someone smaller and more damaged than the one who existed before.

When Rafiq spoke about the event that forced him to flee his home country, his account came in fragments. He would begin, stop, and press his fingers together as if trying to hold onto something slippery and unbearable. He said more than once that he could not seem to put the worst of it into words. What emerged over several sessions was that he had lived through a violent attack in which people around him were badly injured and some did not survive. He remembered visible wounds with terrible clarity: blood, torn flesh, bodies on the ground, the helplessness of seeing who needed help and not being able to stop what was happening. The scene itself seemed to return to him more as images and bodily states than as a full story. At times he could describe a piece of it in a flat, almost detached way, as if he were talking about something that had happened to a stranger. Then, with little warning, the numbness would break and he would be overcome by grief so intense that he had to stop speaking altogether.

From the beginning, what stayed with him was not only horror but guilt. He had come to believe that he should have done more, though he struggled to say what exactly would have been possible in the chaos. He returned repeatedly to the thought that others died and he did not, and there was shame in that fact that he could not reason away. In his mind, survival itself had become an accusation. He said he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, and over the years this had hardened into a broader conclusion that the event had permanently changed him for the worse.

In daily life, the world had narrowed around specific signs of danger. Ambulances were especially difficult. Even now, the rising siren could make his body tighten before he had time to think, and if he saw an ambulance stopped with its back doors open he would feel a sharp urge to get away. Discussions about accidents were almost as bad. In the restaurant, when line cooks casually talked about a highway crash or a delivery driver getting hurt, Rafiq would go quiet and find a reason to move to another station. Seeing visible injuries on other people could unsettle him for hours; even a customer with a bandaged hand or a delivery worker with a fresh cut could pull his attention away from what he was doing and leave him distracted, struggling to focus on orders and timing.

His work as a chef gave him routines, but it also revealed how much of his day was organized around feeling exposed or trapped. Before he relaxed anywhere, even in familiar places, he automatically located exits. In the kitchen he noticed the back door, the service entrance, the narrow route past the prep table without consciously deciding to. When staff gathered outside on break in the open alley behind the restaurant, he often stayed near the doorway rather than stepping into the exposed space. Outdoor festivals or open plazas were worse; he felt too visible there, too vulnerable, and would either avoid them entirely or remain on edge until he could leave.

Uniforms were another problem. Military or police uniforms immediately changed his posture and expression. He became deferential, overly agreeable, eager not to attract attention. He recognized this in himself with some embarrassment. If an officer came into the restaurant, Rafiq was the first to say yes, of course, whatever you need. He did not experience this as politeness so much as something urgent and automatic, a way of keeping himself safe.

Over months and years, these habits had accumulated consequences. At work his concentration suffered when something reminded him of the attack, and coworkers sometimes experienced him as distant or distracted. Outside work he kept his world small, declining invitations that involved crowded public spaces or long walks through open areas. He remained single and increasingly isolated, telling himself that keeping to himself was easier than having to explain why certain ordinary things—a siren, a uniform, a glimpse of blood—could change his entire day.

He finally sought help after a recent shift when an ambulance stopped near the restaurant and two paramedics lifted out someone who was visibly injured. Rafiq froze at the pass, then moved through the rest of service in a haze, numb and mechanically competent until he got home and was hit by a wave of grief so powerful he could not sleep. That episode frightened him not because it was new, but because it felt so familiar and so enduring. He came in saying he was afraid this was all he would ever be now: watchful, guilty, damaged, and unable to speak the worst of what happened. At the same time, he said quietly that he hoped for one thing that still felt almost out of reach—that he might remember and still remain in the present, without losing himself to numbness or grief.
